title: Der gelernte Jäger
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 111. Text from Wikisource („Der gelernte Jäger (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 111 sends a young locksmith's son to apprentice himself to a huntsman instead, and he leaves that trade with an air-gun that never misses. Guided across a lake past a giants' guard-dog, he lets himself into their castle, spares the sleeping princess he finds there, and takes only proof that he was ever in the room — a slipper, a corner of her embroidered neckerchief, a scrap of her shift — before beheading the three giants outside and cutting out their tongues as further evidence. A one-eyed captain claims the rescue for himself and is nearly given the princess in marriage; she is punished for refusing him, first ruined at a pottery stall by wagons sent to smash her wares, then set up alone in a forest cook-house with a sign offering food free one day, for money the next. It is there that the real huntsman finds her again, and the tongues the captain cannot produce — because the giants' mouths are empty — settle the matter at the wedding feast itself. Spelling follows the 1857 edition, so you will meet older forms such as daß, gieng, fieng, ward, thun and todt.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein junger Bursch, der hatte die Schlosserhandtierung gelernt und sprach zu seinem Vater er wollte jetzt in die Welt gehen und sich versuchen.
sentences.l: There was once a young lad, he had learned the locksmith’s-trade and said to his father he wanted now to go into the world and try himself.
sentences.i: Once there was a young lad who had learned the locksmith’s trade, and he told his father that he meant now to go out into the world and try his fortune.
sentences.n: Es war einmal is the fixed opening of a German tale — literally “it was once,” our “once upon a time.” der hatte is a demonstrative picking up ein junger Bursch, not a relative pronoun, so the German runs on where English would subordinate. Schlosserhandtierung is an old word for a line of work, from hantieren, to handle; modern German would say Schlosserhandwerk. sich versuchen is “to try oneself,” to see what one can do.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ sagte der Vater, „das bin ich zufrieden“ und gab ihm etwas Geld auf die Reise.
sentences.l: “Yes,” said the father, “with that I am content” and gave him some money for the journey.
sentences.i: “Yes,” said the father, “I am content with that,” and gave him some money for the journey.
sentences.n: das bin ich zufrieden is an older construction with a bare accusative where modern German says damit bin ich zufrieden. auf die Reise is “for the journey,” money to travel on.

sentences.t: Also zog er herum und suchte Arbeit.
sentences.l: So he moved about and looked for work.
sentences.i: So he wandered about and looked for work.
sentences.n: Also at the head of a sentence is “so, accordingly,” never English “also.” herumziehen is separable, to move about the country — the ordinary life of a journeyman.

sentences.t: Auf eine Zeit, da wollt ihm das Schlosserwerk nicht mehr folgen und stand ihm auch nicht mehr an, aber er kriegte Lust zur Jägerei.
sentences.l: At one time, then the locksmith’s-work would follow him no longer and also suited him no longer, but he got a liking for hunting.
sentences.i: There came a time when the locksmith’s work would no longer go right for him and no longer suited him either, but he took a liking to hunting.
sentences.n: Auf eine Zeit is an old turn, “at a certain time.” folgen here is not the ordinary “to follow”: the work will not obey his hand. The idiom is uncommon, and the reading rests on the clause beside it, stand ihm auch nicht mehr an. anstehen with the dative is “to suit, to please,” and it is separable: stand … an. Lust zu etwas kriegen is “to get a liking for.”

sentences.t: Da begegnete ihm auf der Wanderschaft ein Jäger in grünem Kleide, der fragte wo er her käme und wo er hin wollte.
sentences.l: Then there met him on his wandering a huntsman in green clothing, who asked where he came from and where he wanted to go.
sentences.i: Then on his travels a huntsman in green clothes met him, who asked where he came from and where he was going.
sentences.n: begegnen takes the dative, ihm, so what English makes an object is the German indirect object. Wanderschaft is the journeyman’s years on the road, a stage of the trade itself. wo … her and wo … hin send their directional words to the end of the clause, “whence” and “whither.” Green is the huntsman’s colour throughout these tales.

sentences.t: Er wär ein Schlossergesell, sagte der Bursch, aber das Handwerk gefiele ihm nicht mehr, und hätte Lust zur Jägerei, ob er ihn als Lehrling annehmen wollte.
sentences.l: He was a locksmith’s-journeyman, said the lad, but the trade pleased him no more, and [he] had a liking for hunting, whether he would take him on as an apprentice.
sentences.i: He was a locksmith’s journeyman, said the lad, but the trade no longer pleased him, and he had a mind for hunting — would the huntsman take him on as an apprentice?
sentences.n: wär, gefiele, hätte and wollte are all subjunctive: this is reported speech throughout, and German marks it by the verb alone, with no “he said that.” The subject of hätte is simply dropped, so the literal supplies [he] in brackets. gefallen takes the dative of the person pleased.

sentences.t: „O ja, wenn du mit mir gehen willst.“
sentences.l: “Oh yes, if you want to go with me.”
sentences.i: “Oh yes, if you will come with me.”
sentences.n: mitgehen is separable, and its mit stands just before the infinitive at the end. willst is wollen, “want, are willing,” not a future.

sentences.t: Da gieng der junge Bursch mit, vermiethete sich etliche Jahre bei ihm und lernte die Jägerei.
sentences.l: Then the young lad went along, hired himself out to him for several years and learned the hunter’s craft.
sentences.i: So the young lad went along, hired himself to him for several years and learned the huntsman’s craft.
sentences.n: gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging, and vermiethete of vermietete. sich vermiethen is to hire oneself out for service. etliche is an older word for “several.”

sentences.t: Danach wollte er sich weiter versuchen, und der Jäger gab ihm nichts zum Lohn als eine Windbüchse, die hatte aber die Eigenschaft, wenn er damit einen Schuß that, so traf er ohnfehlbar.
sentences.l: After that he wanted to try himself further, and the huntsman gave him nothing for wages but an air-gun, but it had the property, when he fired a shot with it, then he hit unfailingly.
sentences.i: After that he wanted to try further afield, and the huntsman gave him nothing for wages but an air-gun; it had this property, however, that when he fired a shot with it he hit his mark without fail.
sentences.n: nichts … als is “nothing but.” A Windbüchse is an air-gun, worked by compressed air — a real weapon of the time, and a marvel here. einen Schuß thun is “to fire a shot,” with thun, the 1857 spelling of tun, standing in for a more particular verb. ohnfehlbar is the older form of unfehlbar.

sentences.t: Da gieng er fort und kam in einen sehr großen Wald, von dem konnte er in einem Tag das Ende nicht finden.
sentences.l: Then he went off and came into a very great forest, of which he could not find the end in one day.
sentences.i: Then he went off and came into a very great forest, whose end he could not find in a single day.
sentences.n: von dem keeps the preposition with its relative pronoun at the head of the clause; English lets the preposition fall to the end, or turns to “whose.” fortgehen is separable.

sentences.t: Wies Abend war, setzte er sich auf einen hohen Baum, damit er aus den wilden Thieren käme.
sentences.l: When it was evening, he set himself up on a high tree, so that he might come out from among the wild beasts.
sentences.i: When evening came he settled himself in a high tree, so as to be out of the reach of the wild beasts.
sentences.n: Wies is wie es run together, and wie here means “when,” not “how” — you will meet it constantly in these tales. Thieren is the 1857 spelling of Tieren. aus den wilden Thieren kommen is compressed even for German: to get out from among them, out of their reach. The subjunctive käme marks the clause as one of purpose.

sentences.t: Gegen Mitternacht zu, däuchte ihn, schimmerte ein kleines Lichtchen von weitem, da sah er durch die Äste darauf hin und behielt in acht wo es war.
sentences.l: Toward midnight, it seemed to him, a little light glimmered from far off, then he looked through the branches over toward it and kept in mind where it was.
sentences.i: Toward midnight, so it seemed to him, a little light glimmered far off; he looked out through the branches toward it and kept in mind where it was.
sentences.n: däuchte ihn is an old impersonal from dünken, “it seemed to him”; modern German would say es dünkte ihn. Gegen … zu doubles the preposition, “toward,” a country turn. Lichtchen is the diminutive of Licht. in acht behalten is the set phrase for keeping something in view or in mind.

sentences.t: Doch nahm er erst noch seinen Hut und warf ihn nach dem Licht zu herunter, daß er danach gehen wollte, wann er herabgestiegen wäre, als nach einem Zeichen.
sentences.l: Yet he took first his hat and threw it down toward the light, so that he might go by it, when he had climbed down, as by a sign.
sentences.i: But first he took his hat and threw it down in the direction of the light, so that when he had climbed down he might go by it as by a mark.
sentences.n: nach … zu doubles the direction again, “toward.” daß here stands for damit, “so that.” wann is used where modern German writes wenn. The last phrase, als nach einem Zeichen, reaches back to danach gehen — he will steer by the hat as by a mark.

sentences.t: Nun kletterte er herunter, gieng auf seinen Hut los, setzte ihn wieder auf und zog gerades Wegs fort.
sentences.l: Now he climbed down, made straight for his hat, set it on again and moved off by a straight way.
sentences.i: Now he climbed down, made straight for his hat, put it on again and went off the shortest way.
sentences.n: losgehen auf is “to make for” something. aufsetzen, of a hat, is to put it on. gerades Wegs is an adverbial genitive, “by a straight road,” hence directly.

sentences.t: Je weiter er gieng, je größer ward das Licht,
sentences.l: The further he went, the greater the light became,
sentences.i: The further he went, the greater the light grew,
sentences.n: je … je is the older form of the modern je … desto, “the … the.” ward is the old past of werden, where modern German says wurde.

sentences.t: und wie er nahe dabei kam, sah er daß es ein gewaltiges Feuer war, und saßen drei Riesen dabei und hatten einen Ochsen am Spieß und ließen ihn braten.
sentences.l: and when he came near it, he saw that it was a huge fire, and there sat three giants by it and had an ox on the spit and let it roast.
sentences.i: and when he came near it he saw that it was a great fire, and three giants sat by it with an ox on the spit, letting it roast.
sentences.n: The tale slides out of the daß-clause into plain main clauses and drops their subject, which is why saßen comes first with nothing before it; German narrative does this and English cannot follow it exactly. braten lassen is lassen with a bare infinitive, “to let roast.”

sentences.t: Nun sprach der eine „ich muß doch schmecken ob das Fleisch bald zu essen ist,“
sentences.l: Now the one said “I must taste whether the meat is soon to be eaten,”
sentences.i: Then one of them said, “I must taste whether the meat is nearly fit to eat,”
sentences.n: der eine is “the one of them.” doch is a nudge here, “I really must.” zu essen ist is a passive-flavoured construction, “is to be eaten,” meaning fit to eat.

sentences.t: riß ein Stück herab und wollt es in den Mund stecken, aber der Jäger schoß es ihm aus der Hand.
sentences.l: tore a piece down and wanted to put it into the mouth, but the huntsman shot it out of his hand.
sentences.i: tore a piece off and was about to put it in his mouth, but the huntsman shot it out of his hand.
sentences.n: herabreißen is separable. wollt drops its final -e, as the tales often do in speech and in brisk narrative. ihm aus der Hand is a dative of possession with a plain article — German says “out of the hand to him,” English “out of his hand.”

sentences.t: „Nun ja,“ sprach der Riese, „da weht mir der Wind das Stück aus der Hand“ und nahm sich ein anderes.
sentences.l: “Well now,” said the giant, “there the wind blows the piece out of my hand” and took himself another.
sentences.i: “Well now,” said the giant, “the wind is blowing the piece out of my hand,” and took another.
sentences.n: Again mir … aus der Hand, the dative of possession. sich nehmen has a dative reflexive, “to take for oneself,” which English simply drops.

sentences.t: Wie er eben anbeißen wollte, schoß es ihm der Jäger abermals weg;
sentences.l: When he was just going to bite into it, the huntsman shot it away from him once more;
sentences.i: Just as he was about to bite into it, the huntsman shot it away from him again;
sentences.n: anbeißen, separable, is to take the first bite of a thing. eben is “just, at that very moment.” wegschießen is separable too, and its weg goes to the end of the clause. abermals is an old-fashioned “once again.”

sentences.t: da gab der Riese dem, der neben ihm saß, eine Ohrfeige und rief zornig „was reißt du mir mein Stück weg?“
sentences.l: then the giant gave the one who sat next to him a box on the ear and cried angrily “what do you tear my piece away from me for?”
sentences.i: at that the giant boxed the ear of the one sitting next to him and cried angrily, “What are you snatching my piece away from me for?”
sentences.n: dem, der is “to the one who” — a demonstrative in the dative with a relative clause hanging on it. was here is not “what” as an object but “why, what for,” an older use. wegreißen is separable, and mir is the dative of the person concerned, doubled by mein.

sentences.t: „Ich habe es nicht weggerissen,“ sprach der andere, „es wird dirs ein Scharfschütz weggeschossen haben.“
sentences.l: “I have not torn it away,” said the other, “a sharpshooter will have shot it away from you.”
sentences.i: “I did not snatch it away,” said the other. “Some sharpshooter must have shot it away from you.”
sentences.n: dirs is dir es run together, “it from you.” wird … weggeschossen haben is the future perfect used for a guess about the past, where English says “must have.” A Scharfschütz is a marksman, one who shoots sharp; the fuller form Scharfschütze comes in the next speech.

sentences.t: Der Riese nahm sich das dritte Stück, konnte es aber nicht in der Hand behalten, der Jäger schoß es ihm heraus.
sentences.l: The giant took himself the third piece, could however not keep it in the hand, the huntsman shot it out from him.
sentences.i: The giant took a third piece, but could not keep it in his hand — the huntsman shot it out.
sentences.n: The three attempts are the threefold rhythm these tales like. herausschießen is separable, and ihm is once more the dative of the person it happens to.

sentences.t: Da sprachen die Riesen „das muß ein guter Schütze sein, der den Bissen vor dem Maul wegschießt, so einer wäre uns nützlich,“
sentences.l: Then the giants said “that must be a good marksman, who shoots the morsel away from before the mouth, such a one would be useful to us,”
sentences.i: Then the giants said, “That must be a good marksman, who shoots the morsel away from before one’s mouth; such a one would be useful to us,”
sentences.n: der Bissen is a mouthful, a morsel. Maul is the mouth of an animal, and used of a person it is rough — the giants’ own word for themselves. so einer is “such a one.” nützlich takes the dative, uns.

sentences.t: und riefen laut „komm herbei, du Scharfschütze, setze dich zu uns ans Feuer und iß dich satt, wir wollen dir nichts thun;
sentences.l: and called aloud “come here, you sharpshooter, sit yourself down with us by the fire and eat yourself full, we will do you nothing;
sentences.i: and called aloud, “Come here, sharpshooter, sit down with us by the fire and eat your fill; we mean you no harm;
sentences.n: du Scharfschütze is a vocative — German keeps the pronoun where English drops it. sich satt essen is “to eat oneself full,” our “eat one’s fill.” herbeikommen is separable. wir wollen dir nichts thun is the set assurance, “we mean you no harm.”

sentences.t: aber kommst du nicht, und wir holen dich mit Gewalt, so bist du verloren.“
sentences.l: but if you do not come, and we fetch you by force, then you are lost.”
sentences.i: but if you do not come, and we have to fetch you by force, then you are lost.”
sentences.n: kommst du nicht is a condition built without wenn — German can make one by putting the verb first — and the so that follows answers it. mit Gewalt is “by force.”

sentences.t: Da trat der Bursch herzu und sagte er wäre ein gelernter Jäger, und wonach er mit seiner Büchse ziele, das treffe er auch sicher und gewis.
sentences.l: Then the lad stepped up and said he was a trained huntsman, and whatever he aimed at with his gun, that he hit surely and certainly too.
sentences.i: Then the lad stepped up and said that he was a trained huntsman, and that whatever he aimed at with his gun he hit surely and without fail.
sentences.n: gelernt said of a person means trained, apprenticed, one who has served his years — not “learned” in the sense of erudite; the tale’s title turns on the word. wonach … das is the old correlative, “whatever … that.” wäre, ziele, treffe are all subjunctive, marking reported speech. gewis is printed with one s where modern German writes gewiss.

sentences.t: Da sprachen sie wenn er mit ihnen gehen wollte, sollte ers gut haben,
sentences.l: Then they said if he wanted to go with them, he should have it good,
sentences.i: Then they said that if he would go with them he should be well off,
sentences.n: es gut haben is the set phrase for being well off; ers is er es run together. The reported clause again stands in the subjunctive, sollte.

sentences.t: und erzählten ihm vor dem Wald sei ein großes Wasser, dahinter ständ ein Thurm, und in dem Thurm säß eine schöne Königstochter, die wollten sie gern rauben.
sentences.l: and told him before the forest was a great water, behind it stood a tower, and in the tower sat a beautiful king’s-daughter, whom they would gladly steal.
sentences.i: and told him that in front of the forest there lay a great water, and behind it stood a tower, and in the tower sat a beautiful king’s daughter whom they had a mind to carry off.
sentences.n: sei, ständ, säß are subjunctives of reported speech, running one after another with no “that” to introduce them. Thurm is the 1857 spelling of Turm. Wasser here is a stretch of water, a lake or a broad river. gern rauben is “to like to steal” — German often says wanting to do a thing with a verb plus gern.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ sprach er, „die will ich bald geschafft haben.“
sentences.l: “Yes,” said he, “that one I will soon have got hold of.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” said he, “I shall soon have got her for you.”
sentences.n: die is a demonstrative object thrown to the front, “that one.” schaffen has here its older sense of procuring or bringing; geschafft haben with will makes a future perfect, “I shall soon have got her.”

sentences.t: Sagten sie weiter „es ist aber noch etwas dabei, es liegt ein kleines Hündchen dort,
sentences.l: Said they further “but there is still something in it, there lies a little dog there,
sentences.i: They said further, “But there is something more to it: a little dog lies there,
sentences.n: The verb comes first with no Da or Und before it — a brisk narrative habit of these tales that English cannot copy without sounding odd. es ist etwas dabei is “there is something to it, a catch in it.” Hündchen is the diminutive of Hund.

sentences.t: das fängt gleich an zu bellen, wann sich jemand nähert, und sobald das bellt, wacht auch alles am königlichen Hofe auf:
sentences.l: it begins at once to bark, when anyone approaches, and as soon as it barks, everything at the royal court wakes up too:
sentences.i: and it begins to bark at once when anyone comes near, and as soon as it barks the whole royal court wakes up as well:
sentences.n: das is the pronoun for Hündchen, which is neuter because every -chen diminutive is; English wants “it.” anfangen and aufwachen are both separable — fängt … an, wacht … auf. sich nähern is reflexive, and wann again stands where modern German writes wenn.

sentences.t: und deshalb können wir nicht hinein kommen; unterstehst du dich das Hündchen todt zu schießen?“
sentences.l: and therefore we cannot get in; do you dare to shoot the little dog dead?”
sentences.i: and that is why we cannot get in. Do you dare shoot the little dog dead?”
sentences.n: sich unterstehen is reflexive, to dare or presume to do a thing. todt schießen is “to shoot dead”; todt is the 1857 spelling of tot.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ sprach er, „das ist mir ein kleiner Spaß.“
sentences.l: “Yes,” said he, “that is a small jest to me.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” said he, “that is a small matter to me.”
sentences.n: mir is a dative of the person judging, “as I see it.” Spaß is fun or a jest; here it is a boast — the thing is nothing to him.

sentences.t: Danach setzte er sich auf ein Schiff und fuhr über das Wasser,
sentences.l: After that he set himself onto a boat and went over the water,
sentences.i: After that he got into a boat and went across the water,
sentences.n: sich setzen is reflexive, “to set oneself.” fahren is to travel by some conveyance rather than on foot — here by boat.

sentences.t: und wie er bald beim Land war, kam das Hündlein gelaufen und wollte bellen, aber er kriegte seine Windbüchse und schoß es todt.
sentences.l: and when he was soon at the land, the little dog came running and wanted to bark, but he got his air-gun and shot it dead.
sentences.i: and when he was nearly at the shore, the little dog came running and made to bark, but he took up his air-gun and shot it dead.
sentences.n: kam … gelaufen is a past participle with kommen, the German way of joining motion and manner: “came running.” Hündlein is another diminutive of Hund, beside the Hündchen used a moment ago; the tale uses both freely. kriegen is a plain, homely word for getting hold of a thing.

sentences.t: Wie die Riesen das sahen, freuten sie sich und meinten sie hätten die Königstochter schon gewiß,
sentences.l: When the giants saw that, they rejoiced and thought they had the king’s-daughter already for certain,
sentences.i: When the giants saw that they rejoiced and thought they had the king’s daughter for certain already,
sentences.n: sich freuen is reflexive, “to be glad.” meinen is to be of the opinion, not “to mean.” hätten is subjunctive — the thought is theirs, and the tale is about to show them wrong.

sentences.t: aber der Jäger wollte erst sehen wie die Sache beschaffen war, und sprach sie sollten haußen bleiben, bis er sie riefe.
sentences.l: but the huntsman wanted first to see how the matter was constituted, and said they should stay outside until he called them.
sentences.i: but the huntsman wanted to see first how the matter stood, and said they should stay outside until he called them.
sentences.n: wie eine Sache beschaffen ist is the set phrase for how something stands or is made up. haußen is an old country form of draußen, outside. riefe is subjunctive in the reported clause.

sentences.t: Da gieng er in das Schloß, und es war mäuschenstill darin, und schlief alles.
sentences.l: Then he went into the castle, and it was mouse-still inside, and everything slept.
sentences.i: Then he went into the castle, and it was still as a mouse inside, and everything was asleep.
sentences.n: mäuschenstill, “little-mouse-still,” is the German for dead quiet, built on the diminutive of Maus. The last clause drops its subject to the end, und schlief alles, where English wants “and everything was asleep.”

sentences.t: Wie er das erste Zimmer aufmachte, hieng da ein Säbel an der Wand, der war von purem Silber, und war ein goldener Stern darauf und des Königs Name;
sentences.l: When he opened the first room, there hung a sabre on the wall, it was of pure silver, and there was a golden star on it and the king’s name;
sentences.i: When he opened the first room, there hung a sabre on the wall; it was of pure silver, and there was a golden star on it, and the king’s name;
sentences.n: hieng is the 1857 spelling of hing. purem Silber is plain High German, “pure silver.” des Königs Name puts the genitive in front of its noun, an old order that English keeps in “the king’s name.”

sentences.t: daneben aber lag auf einem Tisch ein versiegelter Brief, den brach er auf, und es stand darin wer den Säbel hätte, könnte alles ums Leben bringen, was ihm vorkäme.
sentences.l: but beside it there lay on a table a sealed letter, that he broke open, and there stood in it whoever had the sabre could bring everything to death that came before him.
sentences.i: but beside it, on a table, lay a sealed letter; he broke it open, and in it stood written that whoever had the sabre could kill whatever came before him.
sentences.n: einen Brief aufbrechen is to break a letter’s seal. es stand darin is the German for “it was written there.” ums Leben bringen is the set phrase for killing. hätte, könnte, vorkäme are subjunctives — the letter’s words reported.

sentences.t: Da nahm er den Säbel von der Wand, hieng ihn um und gieng weiter:
sentences.l: Then he took the sabre from the wall, hung it about him and went further:
sentences.i: Then he took the sabre from the wall, slung it about him and went on:
sentences.n: umhängen is separable, to hang a thing round oneself — a sword-belt over the shoulder.

sentences.t: da kam er in das Zimmer, wo die Königstochter lag und schlief:
sentences.l: then he came into the room where the king’s-daughter lay and slept:
sentences.i: and he came into the room where the king’s daughter lay asleep:
sentences.n: liegen und schlafen doubled is the tale’s way of saying she lay sleeping; German prefers the two plain verbs. The colon works as a soft full stop, as it does throughout this printing.

sentences.t: und sie war so schön, daß er still stand und sie betrachtete und den Athem anhielt.
sentences.l: and she was so beautiful that he stood still and looked at her and held the breath.
sentences.i: and she was so beautiful that he stood still and gazed at her and held his breath.
sentences.n: den Athem anhalten uses the plain article where English wants “his”; Athem is the 1857 spelling of Atem. anhalten is separable. betrachten is to look at with attention.

sentences.t: Er dachte bei sich selbst „wie darf ich eine unschuldige Jungfrau in die Gewalt der wilden Riesen bringen, die haben Böses im Sinn.“
sentences.l: He thought to himself “how may I bring an innocent maiden into the power of the wild giants, they have evil in mind.”
sentences.i: He thought to himself, “How can I bring an innocent maiden into the power of these wild giants? They mean harm.”
sentences.n: bei sich selbst denken is “to think to oneself.” dürfen is permission — “how am I allowed to” — which in this question comes to “how could I.” Böses im Sinn haben is the set phrase for meaning harm. The German prints no question mark, though the sentence asks.

sentences.t: Er schaute sich weiter um, da standen unter dem Bett ein paar Pantoffeln, auf dem rechten stand ihres Vaters Name mit einem Stern und auf dem linken ihr eigener Name mit einem Stern.
sentences.l: He looked further about him, then there stood under the bed a pair of slippers, on the right one stood her father’s name with a star and on the left one her own name with a star.
sentences.i: He looked further about him, and under the bed stood a pair of slippers; on the right one stood her father’s name with a star, and on the left her own name with a star.
sentences.n: sich umschauen is reflexive and separable, “to look about oneself.” stehen is the German verb for what is written on a thing — a name stands on it. ihres Vaters Name again puts the genitive first.

sentences.t: Sie hatte auch ein großes Halstuch um, von Seide mit Gold ausgestickt, auf der rechten Seite ihres Vaters Name, auf der linken ihr Name, alles mit goldenen Buchstaben.
sentences.l: She had also a great neck-cloth about her, of silk embroidered with gold, on the right side her father’s name, on the left hers, all in golden letters.
sentences.i: She had a great silk neckerchief about her too, embroidered with gold, her father’s name on the right side, her own on the left, all in golden letters.
sentences.n: umhaben is separable — hatte … um, “had about her.” The clauses that follow have no verb at all; German lets the list stand bare, and English can follow it. ausgestickt is the past participle of aussticken, to work in embroidery.

sentences.t: Da nahm der Jäger eine Scheere und schnitt den rechten Schlippen ab und that ihn in seinen Ranzen,
sentences.l: Then the huntsman took a pair of scissors and cut the right corner off and put it into his knapsack,
sentences.i: Then the huntsman took a pair of scissors, cut off the right corner and put it into his knapsack,
sentences.n: Scheere is the 1857 spelling of Schere, and one German word covers what English calls a pair of scissors. Der Schlippen is a regional word, thinly recorded; “the hanging corner or tip of a cloth” is what the tale requires of it here, and what the neckerchief in the next lines confirms. abschneiden is separable; that is the 1857 past of thun, modern tat.

sentences.t: und dann nahm er auch den rechten Pantoffel mit des Königs Namen und steckte ihn hinein.
sentences.l: and then he took also the right slipper with the king’s name and put it in.
sentences.i: and then he took the right slipper too, with the king’s name on it, and put that in as well.
sentences.n: hineinstecken is separable, its hinein waiting at the end of the clause. He is gathering Wahrzeichen, tokens that will prove later who did the deed.

sentences.t: Nun lag die Jungfrau noch immer und schlief, und sie war ganz in ihr Hemd eingenäht:
sentences.l: Now the maiden still lay and slept, and she was sewn entirely into her shift:
sentences.i: Now the maiden still lay sleeping, and she was sewn up entirely in her shift:
sentences.n: einnähen is separable, to sew someone or something in. Being sewn into one’s night-shift was a real practice, and here it is also what lets him cut away a scrap without touching her.

sentences.t: da schnitt er auch ein Stückchen von dem Hemd ab und steckte es zu dem andern, doch that er das alles ohne sie anzurühren.
sentences.l: so he cut a little piece off the shift too and put it with the others, yet he did all that without touching her.
sentences.i: so he cut a little piece from the shift as well and put it with the rest, and yet he did all this without touching her.
sentences.n: ohne … zu is the ohne-zu construction, “without doing”; anrühren is separable, so the zu sits inside it, anzurühren. Stückchen is the diminutive of Stück. The tale is careful to say he does not touch her — it is what sets him apart from the giants.

sentences.t: Dann gieng er fort und ließ sie ungestört schlafen, und als er wieder ans Thor kam, standen die Riesen noch draußen, warteten auf ihn und dachten er würde die Königstochter bringen.
sentences.l: Then he went off and let her sleep undisturbed, and when he came to the gate again, the giants still stood outside, waited for him and thought he would bring the king’s-daughter.
sentences.i: Then he went off and let her sleep undisturbed, and when he came back to the gate the giants were still standing outside, waiting for him and thinking he would bring the king’s daughter.
sentences.n: warten auf takes the accusative, “to wait for.” German sets the three past-tense verbs side by side where English turns the last two into participles. Thor is the 1857 spelling of Tor, a gate.

sentences.t: Er rief ihnen aber zu sie sollten herein kommen, die Jungfrau wäre schon in seiner Gewalt:
sentences.l: But he called out to them they should come in, the maiden was already in his power:
sentences.i: But he called out to them that they should come in, that the maiden was already in his power:
sentences.n: zurufen is separable and takes the dative — rief ihnen … zu, “called out to them.” sollten and wäre are subjunctives of reported speech; he is lying to them, and the subjunctive keeps the words his.

sentences.t: die Thüre könnte er ihnen aber nicht aufmachen, aber da wäre ein Loch, durch welches sie kriechen müßten.
sentences.l: the door he could not open for them, but there was a hole through which they would have to crawl.
sentences.i: he could not open the door for them, but there was a hole through which they would have to crawl.
sentences.n: The object stands first once more: die Thüre könnte er … The dative ihnen is “for them.” welches is the older relative pronoun where modern German would use das. Thüre is the 1857 spelling of Türe.

sentences.t: Nun kam der erste näher, da wickelte der Jäger des Riesen Haar um seine Hand,
sentences.l: Now the first came nearer, then the huntsman wound the giant’s hair about his hand,
sentences.i: Now the first came nearer, and the huntsman wound the giant’s hair about his hand,
sentences.n: des Riesen Haar is the genitive standing before its noun again. um etwas wickeln is to wind a thing round something.

sentences.t: zog den Kopf herein und hieb ihn mit seinem Säbel in einem Streich ab, und duns (zog) ihn dann vollends hinein.
sentences.l: drew the head in and struck it off with his sabre at one stroke, and duns (drew) him then wholly in.
sentences.i: drew the head in and struck it off at a single stroke with his sabre, and then hauled him right in.
sentences.n: in einem Streich is “at one stroke.” duns is a regional form otherwise barely recorded; we know what it means only because the 1857 text glosses it on the spot — the round brackets and the word zog inside them are printed in the edition and are the Grimms’ own, not anything supplied here. abhauen and hineinziehen are both separable.

sentences.t: Dann rief er den zweiten und hieb ihm gleichfalls das Haupt ab, und endlich auch dem dritten,
sentences.l: Then he called the second and struck the head off him likewise, and at last off the third too,
sentences.i: Then he called the second and struck his head off likewise, and at last the third’s as well,
sentences.n: ihm … das Haupt abhauen is the dative of possession — “strike the head off him” — which is why the third giant appears in the dative too, dem dritten. Haupt is the higher word for head, beside the plain Kopf used a moment ago.

sentences.t: und war froh daß er die schöne Jungfrau von ihren Feinden befreit hatte und schnitt ihnen die Zungen aus und steckte sie in seinen Ranzen.
sentences.l: and was glad that he had freed the beautiful maiden from her enemies and cut the tongues out of them and put them in his knapsack.
sentences.i: and he was glad that he had freed the beautiful maiden from her enemies, and he cut out their tongues and put them in his knapsack.
sentences.n: ihnen die Zungen ausschneiden is once more the dative of possession, “cut the tongues out of them.” ausschneiden is separable. The tongues will be the proof at the end of the tale.

sentences.t: Da dachte er „ich will heim gehen zu meinem Vater und ihm zeigen was ich schon gethan habe, dann will ich in der Welt herum ziehen;
sentences.l: Then he thought “I will go home to my father and show him what I have already done, then I will move about in the world;
sentences.i: Then he thought, “I will go home to my father and show him what I have done already, and then I will travel about the world;
sentences.n: will is wollen, “I intend,” not the future. heim gehen and herum ziehen are separable verbs printed here as two words, as this edition often does. gethan is the 1857 spelling of getan.

sentences.t: das Glück, das mir Gott bescheeren will, wird mich schon erreichen.“
sentences.l: the good fortune that God will bestow on me will reach me right enough.”
sentences.i: the good fortune God means to grant me will find me soon enough.”
sentences.n: bescheeren is the 1857 spelling of bescheren, to grant or bestow as a gift — the word used of what is laid out at Christmas. schon here is not “already” but a reassurance, “right enough, never fear.”

sentences.t: Der König in dem Schloß aber, als er aufwachte, erblickte er die drei Riesen, die da todt lagen.
sentences.l: But the king in the castle, when he woke up, he caught sight of the three giants that lay there dead.
sentences.i: But the king in the castle, when he woke, caught sight of the three giants lying there dead.
sentences.n: The subject is named at the head, Der König, and then taken up again by er after the interrupting clause — a loose joint the tales allow and modern German would not. todt is the 1857 spelling of tot.

sentences.t: Dann gieng er in die Schlafkammer seiner Tochter, weckte sie auf und fragte wer das wohl gewesen wäre, der die Riesen ums Leben gebracht hätte.
sentences.l: Then he went into his daughter’s sleeping-chamber, woke her up and asked who that might have been who had brought the giants to death.
sentences.i: Then he went into his daughter’s bedchamber, woke her and asked who it could have been who had killed the giants.
sentences.n: aufwecken is separable. wohl in a question is a shade of guessing, “who might it have been.” wäre and hätte keep the question in the subjunctive, as reported speech. ums Leben bringen is again the set phrase for killing.

sentences.t: Da sagte sie „lieber Vater, ich weiß es nicht, ich habe geschlafen.“
sentences.l: Then she said “dear father, I do not know, I have slept.”
sentences.i: Then she said, “Dear father, I do not know; I was asleep.”
sentences.n: ich habe geschlafen is the perfect, which German uses in speech where English reaches for a simple past, “I was asleep.” weiß is from wissen, to know.

sentences.t: Wie sie nun aufstand und ihre Pantoffeln anziehen wollte, da war der rechte weg,
sentences.l: When she now got up and wanted to put her slippers on, then the right one was gone,
sentences.i: When she got up and went to put on her slippers, the right one was gone,
sentences.n: aufstehen and anziehen are both separable. weg sein is “to be gone.” The tale now runs back over the tokens the huntsman took, one by one.

sentences.t: und wie sie ihr Halstuch betrachtete, war es durchschnitten und fehlte der rechte Schlippen, und wie sie ihr Hemd ansah, war ein Stückchen heraus.
sentences.l: and when she looked at her neck-cloth, it was cut through and the right corner was missing, and when she looked at her shift, a little piece was out of it.
sentences.i: and when she looked at her neckerchief, it was cut through and the right corner was missing, and when she looked at her shift, a little piece was gone from it.
sentences.n: durchschnitten is the past participle of durchschneiden used as a predicate, “cut through.” fehlen is “to be missing,” with the missing thing as its subject. ansehen is separable.

sentences.t: Der König ließ den ganzen Hof zusammen kommen, Soldaten und alles, was da war, und fragte wer seine Tochter befreit und die Riesen ums Leben gebracht hätte?
sentences.l: The king had the whole court come together, soldiers and everything that was there, and asked who had freed his daughter and brought the giants to death?
sentences.i: The king had the whole court assemble, soldiers and everyone else there was, and asked who had freed his daughter and killed the giants?
sentences.n: zusammen kommen lassen is “to have come together,” lassen with an infinitive. The question mark stands at the end although the question is reported, not quoted — the 1857 printing does this often.

sentences.t: Nun hatte er einen Hauptmann, der war einäugig und ein häßlicher Mensch, der sagte er hätte es gethan.
sentences.l: Now he had a captain, he was one-eyed and an ugly man, he said he had done it.
sentences.i: Now he had a captain, a one-eyed man and an ugly one, and he said that he had done it.
sentences.n: der … der: both are demonstratives picking up the captain, not relative pronouns, so the German runs on in short main clauses. hätte is subjunctive — the claim is his, and the tale does not vouch for it.

sentences.t: Da sprach der alte König so er das vollbracht hätte, sollte er seine Tochter auch heirathen.
sentences.l: Then the old king said if he had accomplished that, he should also marry his daughter.
sentences.i: Then the old king said that if he had accomplished it he should marry his daughter as well.
sentences.n: so at the head of a clause is here the old conditional “if,” not “so.” heirathen is the 1857 spelling of heiraten, and it takes a plain accusative — one marries someone, with no preposition.

sentences.t: Die Jungfrau aber sagte „lieber Vater, dafür, daß ich den heirathen soll, will ich lieber in die Welt gehen, so weit als mich meine Beine tragen.“
sentences.l: But the maiden said “dear father, rather than that I should marry him, I will sooner go out into the world, as far as my legs carry me.”
sentences.i: But the maiden said, “Dear father, sooner than marry him I will go out into the world, as far as my legs will carry me.”
sentences.n: dafür, daß … is “in place of that, rather than that.” lieber is the comparative of gern, “rather, sooner” — beside the lieber Vater at the head, which is the adjective “dear”; the same shape, two different words. den is a demonstrative, “that one,” said of the captain with no warmth in it.

sentences.t: Da sprach der König wenn sie den nicht heirathen wollte, sollte sie die königlichen Kleider ausziehen und Bauernkleider anthun und fortgehen;
sentences.l: Then the king said if she would not marry him, she should take off the royal clothes and put on peasant’s-clothes and go away;
sentences.i: Then the king said that if she would not marry him she should take off her royal clothes, put on peasant’s clothes and go away;
sentences.n: anthun for anziehen is an older way of saying to put on; anthun is the 1857 spelling of antun. ausziehen and fortgehen are separable as well. The royal clothes take the plain article where English wants “her.”

sentences.t: und sie sollte zu einem Töpfer gehen und einen Handel mit irdenem Geschirr anfangen.
sentences.l: and she should go to a potter and begin a trade with earthen vessels.
sentences.i: and she should go to a potter and set up a trade in earthenware.
sentences.n: irden is the adjective “earthen,” of baked clay. einen Handel anfangen is to set up in trade, and anfangen is separable.

sentences.t: Da that sie ihre königlichen Kleider aus und gieng zu einem Töpfer und borgte sich einen Kram irden Werk;
sentences.l: So she did her royal clothes off and went to a potter and borrowed herself a stock of earthen ware;
sentences.i: So she took off her royal clothes and went to a potter and borrowed a stock of earthenware;
sentences.n: austhun, “to do off,” is the older separable verb for taking clothes off. Ein Kram is a pedlar’s stock of goods, the whole basketful. irden Werk keeps the old uninflected adjective where modern German would write irdenes Werk.

sentences.t: sie versprach ihm auch, wenn sies am Abend verkauft hätte, wollte sie es bezahlen.
sentences.l: she promised him too, when she had sold it in the evening, she would pay for it.
sentences.i: she promised him too that when she had sold it by evening she would pay him for it.
sentences.n: sies is sie es run together. versprechen takes the dative of the person promised. hätte and wollte are subjunctives — her promise, reported.

sentences.t: Nun sagte der König sie sollte sich an eine Ecke damit setzen und es verkaufen,
sentences.l: Now the king said she should set herself with it at a corner and sell it,
sentences.i: Now the king said she should sit down with it at a street corner and sell it,
sentences.n: sich setzen is reflexive; damit, “with that,” points back to the stock of pots.

sentences.t: dann bestellte er etliche Bauerwagen, die sollten mitten durchfahren, daß alles in tausend Stücke gienge.
sentences.l: then he ordered several peasants’ waggons, they were to drive right through the middle, so that everything should go into a thousand pieces.
sentences.i: then he ordered several peasants’ waggons to drive right through the middle of it, so that everything should go to a thousand pieces.
sentences.n: durchfahren is separable here — mitten durchfahren, “to drive through the middle.” daß again stands for damit, “so that,” and gienge is its subjunctive of purpose. This is the father’s cruelty, told without a word of comment.

sentences.t: Wie nun die Königstochter ihren Kram auf die Straße hingestellt hatte, kamen die Wagen und zerbrachen ihn zu lauter Scherben.
sentences.l: When the king’s-daughter had now set her stock out on the street, the waggons came and broke it to nothing but shards.
sentences.i: When the king’s daughter had set out her stock in the street, the waggons came and broke it all to shards.
sentences.n: hinstellen is separable, to set a thing out or down. lauter is “nothing but, sheer.” Scherben are the broken pieces of pottery.

sentences.t: Sie fieng an zu weinen und sprach „ach Gott wie will ich nun dem Töpfer bezahlen.“
sentences.l: She began to weep and said “ah God, how shall I pay the potter now.”
sentences.i: She began to weep and said, “Ah God, how am I to pay the potter now?”
sentences.n: anfangen is separable — fieng … an; fieng is the 1857 spelling of fing. bezahlen here takes a dative of the person, dem Töpfer, where modern German would put him in the accusative. The German prints no question mark, though the sentence asks.

sentences.t: Der König aber hatte sie damit zwingen wollen den Hauptmann zu heirathen,
sentences.l: But the king had wanted to force her with that to marry the captain,
sentences.i: But the king had meant by this to force her into marrying the captain,
sentences.n: hatte … zwingen wollen is a double infinitive: with a modal, the perfect uses wollen and not gewollt, and both infinitives pile up at the end of the clause. zwingen zu is “to force to.”

sentences.t: statt dessen gieng sie wieder zum Töpfer und fragte ihn ob er ihr noch einmal borgen wollte.
sentences.l: instead of that she went again to the potter and asked him whether he would lend to her once more.
sentences.i: instead she went back to the potter and asked whether he would give her credit once more.
sentences.n: statt dessen is “instead of that.” borgen serves for both lending and borrowing in German; here the potter is the one who would lend, and the person lent to stands in the dative, ihr.

sentences.t: Er antwortete nein, sie sollte erst das Vorige bezahlen.
sentences.l: He answered no, she should first pay for the previous.
sentences.i: He answered no: she should pay for the last lot first.
sentences.n: das Vorige is an adjective used as a noun, “the previous [lot].” The refusal is reported with no “that” at all, only the subjunctive sollte to mark it.

sentences.t: Da gieng sie zu ihrem Vater, schrie und jammerte, und sagte sie wollte in die Welt hineingehen.
sentences.l: Then she went to her father, cried out and lamented, and said she wanted to go into the world.
sentences.i: Then she went to her father, cried out and lamented, and said that she meant to go off into the world.
sentences.n: jammern is to wail or lament aloud. hineingehen, “to go in,” is used here of going out into the wide world — German sees the world as something one enters.

sentences.t: Da sprach er „ich will dir draußen in dem Wald ein Häuschen bauen lassen, darin sollst du dein Lebtag sitzen und für jedermann kochen, du darfst aber kein Geld nehmen.“
sentences.l: Then he said “I will have a little house built for you out there in the forest, in it you shall sit your life long and cook for everyone, but you may take no money.”
sentences.i: Then he said, “I will have a little house built for you out in the forest; in it you shall sit all your life and cook for everyone, but you may take no money.”
sentences.n: bauen lassen — lassen with an infinitive is “to have something done.” dein Lebtag is an accusative of duration, “your life long.” Häuschen is the diminutive of Haus. darfst is permission: “you are not allowed to take money.”

sentences.t: Als das Häuschen fertig war, ward vor die Thüre ein Schild gehängt, darauf stand geschrieben „heute umsonst, morgen für Geld.“
sentences.l: When the little house was ready, a sign was hung before the door, on it stood written “today for nothing, tomorrow for money.”
sentences.i: When the little house was finished, a sign was hung before the door, and on it stood written, “Today free, tomorrow for money.”
sentences.n: ward is the old past of werden, here making the passive. stand geschrieben is the German for “was written there” — the writing stands. umsonst is “for nothing, free of charge”; it can also mean “in vain,” and the tale will lean on the first sense only.

sentences.t: Da saß sie lange Zeit, und sprach es sich in der Welt herum, da säße eine Jungfrau, die kochte umsonst, und das stände vor der Thüre an einem Schild.
sentences.l: There she sat a long time, and it spoke itself about in the world that a maiden sat there who cooked for nothing, and that stood before the door on a sign.
sentences.i: There she sat a long time, and word went round the world that a maiden sat there who cooked for nothing, and that this stood on a sign before her door.
sentences.n: es spricht sich herum is a reflexive impersonal — “it speaks itself around,” our “word gets about”; sich herumsprechen is separable. säße, kochte, stände are subjunctives: this is what people were saying.

sentences.t: Das hörte auch der Jäger und dachte „das wär etwas für dich, du bist doch arm und hast kein Geld.“
sentences.l: The huntsman heard that too and thought “that would be something for you, you are after all poor and have no money.”
sentences.i: The huntsman heard this too and thought, “That would be something for you; you are poor after all and have no money.”
sentences.n: He addresses himself as du — the tales do this often, and it is “you,” not any solemn form. wär is the subjunctive of sein with its -e dropped, “would be.” doch is “after all, when it comes to it.”

sentences.t: Er nahm also seine Windbüchse und seinen Ranzen, worin noch alles steckte, was er damals im Schloß als Wahrzeichen mitgenommen hatte,
sentences.l: So he took his air-gun and his knapsack, in which everything still stuck that he had taken along at that time in the castle as tokens,
sentences.i: So he took his air-gun and his knapsack, in which everything still lay that he had carried off from the castle at the time as tokens,
sentences.n: worin is “wherein,” the relative that saves saying in dem. stecken is to be stuck or lodged somewhere, the plain word for a thing being inside. Ein Wahrzeichen is a token that proves a thing — the whole plot turns on them.

sentences.t: gieng in den Wald und fand auch das Häuschen mit dem Schild „heute umsonst, morgen für Geld.“
sentences.l: went into the forest and found the little house too with the sign “today for nothing, tomorrow for money.”
sentences.i: went into the forest and found the little house too, with the sign, “Today free, tomorrow for money.”
sentences.n: The subject er is not repeated — German runs the second clause on from the first subject, and English can do the same here.

sentences.t: Er hatte aber den Degen umhängen, womit er den drei Riesen den Kopf abgehauen hatte, trat so in das Häuschen hinein und ließ sich etwas zu essen geben.
sentences.l: But he had the sword hanging about him with which he had struck the head off the three giants, stepped so into the little house and had something to eat given to himself.
sentences.i: But he had the sword slung about him with which he had struck off the three giants’ heads, and so he stepped into the little house and had something to eat brought him.
sentences.n: umhängen haben is “to have something hanging about one,” with the participle printed like an infinitive. den drei Riesen den Kopf abgehauen is the dative of possession again. sich etwas geben lassen is “to have something given to oneself.” Degen and Säbel are used of the same weapon here, sword and sabre.

sentences.t: Er freute sich über das schöne Mädchen, es war aber auch bildschön.
sentences.l: He rejoiced over the beautiful girl, and indeed it was picture-beautiful.
sentences.i: He took delight in the beautiful girl — and indeed she was as fair as a picture.
sentences.n: sich freuen über is “to take pleasure in.” es is the pronoun for Mädchen, which is neuter because every -chen diminutive is, so German says “it” of a girl where English will not. bildschön, “picture-beautiful,” is still the ordinary German for as pretty as a picture.

sentences.t: Sie fragte wo er her käme und hin wollte, da sagte er „ich reise in der Welt herum.“
sentences.l: She asked where he came from and wanted to go, then he said “I am travelling about in the world.”
sentences.i: She asked where he came from and where he was going, and he said, “I am travelling about the world.”
sentences.n: wo … her and wo … hin send their directional words to the end of the clause, “whence” and “whither,” as at the beginning of the tale. käme and wollte are subjunctives of reported speech.

sentences.t: Da fragte sie ihn wo er den Degen her hätte, da stände ja ihres Vaters Name darauf.
sentences.l: Then she asked him where he had the sword from, her father’s name stood on it after all.
sentences.i: Then she asked him where he had got the sword, since her father’s name stood on it.
sentences.n: ja inside a clause is not “yes” but a nudge at what both can see — “after all, as you know.” stände is subjunctive, keeping the words hers.

sentences.t: Fragte er ob sie des Königs Tochter wäre.
sentences.l: Asked he whether she was the king’s daughter.
sentences.i: He asked whether she was the king’s daughter.
sentences.n: The verb comes first with nothing before it — the brisk narrative habit met earlier in the tale. ob is “whether,” and wäre is again the reported subjunctive.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ antwortete sie.
sentences.l: “Yes,” she answered.
sentences.n: The bare answer stands alone; the tale is moving fast now toward the recognition.

sentences.t: „Mit diesem Säbel,“ sprach er, „habe ich drei Riesen den Kopf abgehauen“ und holte zum Zeichen ihre Zungen aus dem Ranzen,
sentences.l: “With this sabre,” said he, “I have struck the head off three giants” and fetched their tongues out of the knapsack for a token,
sentences.i: “With this sabre,” said he, “I struck the heads off three giants,” and for a token he fetched their tongues out of his knapsack,
sentences.n: Mit diesem Säbel comes first, so the verb habe stands second and the subject after it — the ordinary German rule. drei Riesen is the dative of possession once more. zum Zeichen is “as a token, in proof.”

sentences.t: dann zeigte er ihr auch den Pantoffel, den Schlippen vom Halstuch und das Stück vom Hemd.
sentences.l: then he showed her the slipper too, the corner from the neck-cloth and the piece from the shift.
sentences.i: then he showed her the slipper as well, the corner of the neckerchief and the piece of the shift.
sentences.n: The three tokens come out in the order he took them; German prefers von where English would use a plain possessive.

sentences.t: Da war sie voll Freude und sagte er wäre derjenige der sie erlöst hätte.
sentences.l: Then she was full of joy and said he was the one who had delivered her.
sentences.i: Then she was full of joy and said that he was the one who had delivered her.
sentences.n: derjenige, der is the emphatic “the one who.” erlösen is to redeem or set free, a heavier word than befreien and the one these tales use for breaking a spell or lifting a doom.

sentences.t: Darauf giengen sie zusammen zum alten König und holten ihn herbei, und sie führte ihn in ihre Kammer und sagte ihm der Jäger wäre der rechte, der sie von den Riesen erlöst hätte.
sentences.l: Thereupon they went together to the old king and fetched him over, and she led him into her chamber and told him the huntsman was the right one who had delivered her from the giants.
sentences.i: Thereupon they went together to the old king and brought him along, and she led him into her chamber and told him that the huntsman was the right man, the one who had delivered her from the giants.
sentences.n: herbeiholen is separable. der rechte is “the right one,” the true one as against the captain’s claim. The reported clause stands in the subjunctive again, wäre, hätte.

sentences.t: Und wie der alte König die Wahrzeichen alle sah, da konnte er nicht mehr zweifeln
sentences.l: And when the old king saw the tokens all, then he could doubt no longer
sentences.i: And when the old king saw all the tokens, he could doubt no longer
sentences.n: die Wahrzeichen alle puts alle after its noun, an older order that gives the word weight; modern German would say alle Wahrzeichen.

sentences.t: und sagte es wäre ihm lieb daß er wüßte wie alles zugegangen wäre, und er sollte sie nun auch zur Gemahlin haben;
sentences.l: and said it was dear to him that he knew how everything had come about, and he should now have her to wife too;
sentences.i: and said that he was glad to know how it had all come about, and that the huntsman should now have her to wife;
sentences.n: es ist mir lieb is the set phrase for being glad of a thing — literally “it is dear to me.” zugehen is “to come about, to happen,” separable, and here in the reported subjunctive. zur Gemahlin haben is the formal phrase for taking a wife, Gemahlin being the high word for one.

sentences.t: darüber freute sich die Jungfrau von Herzen.
sentences.l: over that the maiden rejoiced from the heart.
sentences.i: and at that the maiden rejoiced from her heart.
sentences.n: sich freuen über again, with darüber standing first in the clause. von Herzen is the set phrase, “from the heart, heartily.”

sentences.t: Darauf kleideten sie ihn, als wenn er ein fremder Herr wäre, und der König ließ ein Gastmahl anstellen.
sentences.l: Thereupon they clothed him as if he were a strange gentleman, and the king had a banquet set on.
sentences.i: Thereupon they dressed him as though he were a gentleman from abroad, and the king had a banquet prepared.
sentences.n: als wenn with the subjunctive is “as if.” fremd is strange in the sense of foreign, from elsewhere. ein Gastmahl anstellen is to arrange a feast; anstellen is separable, and lassen again means “to have it done.”

sentences.t: Als sie nun zu Tisch giengen, kam der Hauptmann auf die linke Seite der Königstochter zu sitzen, der Jäger aber auf die rechte:
sentences.l: When they now went to table, the captain came to sit on the left side of the king’s-daughter, the huntsman however on the right:
sentences.i: When they went in to table, the captain came to sit on the king’s daughter’s left, and the huntsman on her right:
sentences.n: zu Tisch gehen is the set phrase for going in to a meal, with no article. zu sitzen kommen is “to come to sit,” to end up seated. The right hand is the place of honour, which is the point of the seating.

sentences.t: und der Hauptmann meinte das wäre ein fremder Herr und wäre zum Besuch gekommen.
sentences.l: and the captain thought that was a strange gentleman and had come on a visit.
sentences.i: and the captain supposed that this was a gentleman from abroad who had come on a visit.
sentences.n: meinen is to suppose or be of the opinion, not “to mean.” The subjunctives wäre … wäre keep the mistake his own.

sentences.t: Wie sie gegessen und getrunken hatten, sprach der alte König zum Hauptmann er wollte ihm etwas aufgeben, das sollte er errathen:
sentences.l: When they had eaten and drunk, the old king said to the captain he wanted to set him something, that he should guess:
sentences.i: When they had eaten and drunk, the old king said to the captain that he would set him something to guess:
sentences.n: aufgeben is separable, to set someone a task or a puzzle. errathen is the 1857 spelling of erraten, to guess out. das is a demonstrative object thrown to the front of its clause.

sentences.t: wenn einer spräche er hätte drei Riesen ums Leben gebracht, und er gefragt würde, wo die Zungen der Riesen wären, und er müßte zusehen, und wären keine in ihren Köpfen, wie das zugienge?
sentences.l: if one were to say he had brought three giants to death, and he were asked where the tongues of the giants were, and he had to look, and there were none in their heads, how would that come about?
sentences.i: if a man were to say that he had killed three giants, and were asked where the giants’ tongues were, and had to go and look, and there were none in their heads — how would that be?
sentences.n: The whole riddle stands in the subjunctive: spräche, hätte, würde, wären, müßte, zugienge — six of them in a row, because the case is only supposed. zusehen is separable, to go and look. The tale prints a question mark although nothing is quoted.

sentences.t: Da sagte der Hauptmann „sie werden keine gehabt haben.“
sentences.l: Then the captain said “they will have had none.”
sentences.i: Then the captain said, “They will not have had any.”
sentences.n: werden … gehabt haben is the future perfect used for a guess about the past — English says “they must not have had any.” It is the answer of a man improvising.

sentences.t: „Nicht so,“ sagte der König, „jedes Gethier hat eine Zunge,“ und fragte weiter was der werth wäre, daß ihm widerführe?
sentences.l: “Not so,” said the king, “every beast has a tongue,” and asked further what that one was worth, that it should befall him?
sentences.i: “Not so,” said the king. “Every creature has a tongue.” And he asked further what such a man deserved should be done to him.
sentences.n: Gethier is the 1857 spelling of Getier, a collective for beasts. werth sein here is “to deserve” rather than “to be worth,” and widerfahren, to befall someone, takes the dative ihm. The German is compressed almost past bearing — what is such a one worth, that it should befall him — and the exact force of daß here is arguable; what the king is asking is plain enough from the answer he gets.

sentences.t: Antwortete der Hauptmann „der gehört in Stücken zerrissen zu werden.“
sentences.l: Answered the captain “that one deserves to be torn in pieces.”
sentences.i: The captain answered, “Such a man deserves to be torn in pieces.”
sentences.n: gehören with a passive infinitive is “to deserve to be” — literally “belongs to be torn.” in Stücken is the older form where modern German would say in Stücke. The captain has just sentenced himself.

sentences.t: Da sagte der König er hätte sich selber sein Urtheil gesprochen,
sentences.l: Then the king said he had spoken his sentence on himself,
sentences.i: Then the king said that he had passed sentence on himself,
sentences.n: sein Urtheil sprechen is the set phrase for passing sentence; Urtheil is the 1857 spelling of Urteil. sich selber is “on himself,” a dative reflexive.

sentences.t: und ward der Hauptmann gefänglich gesetzt und dann in vier Stücke zerrissen, die Königstochter aber mit dem Jäger vermählt.
sentences.l: and the captain was set in prison and then torn into four pieces, the king’s-daughter however wedded to the huntsman.
sentences.i: and the captain was put in prison and then torn into four pieces, while the king’s daughter was wedded to the huntsman.
sentences.n: gefänglich setzen is the old legal phrase for taking into custody. ward is again the old passive auxiliary. The last clause has no verb of its own — it borrows ward … vermählt from what went before, so the two fates are set side by side in one breath, and the tale does not flinch at either.

sentences.t: Danach holte er seinen Vater und seine Mutter herbei, und die lebten in Freude bei ihrem Sohn, und nach des alten Königs Tod bekam er das Reich.
sentences.l: After that he fetched his father and his mother over, and they lived in joy with their son, and after the old king’s death he received the kingdom.
sentences.i: After that he brought his father and his mother to him, and they lived in joy with their son, and after the old king’s death he received the kingdom.
sentences.n: die at the head of the second clause is a demonstrative, “those, they.” des alten Königs Tod is the genitive standing before its noun once more. He had promised at the giants’ fire to go home to his father, and the tale keeps the promise at the end.

glossary.anfangen: anfangen — to begin, to set up (infinitive; separable, fängt an)
glossary.anhielt: anhalten — to hold (3rd sg. past; separable; den Athem anhalten, to hold one’s breath)
glossary.aufstand: aufstehen — got up, rose (3rd sg. past; separable, prefix auf-)
glossary.folgen: folgen — to follow (with the dative; here of work that no longer answers to the hand doing it)
glossary.licht: das Licht — light; also a light one can carry or set down, a lamp or flame
glossary.purem: pur — pure (dat. sg. after von: von purem Silber, of pure silver)
glossary.reißt: reißen — to tear, snatch (2nd sg. present; here wegreißen, with weg at the end of the clause)
glossary.riefe: rufen — to call (3rd sg. past subjunctive of reported speech)
glossary.schmecken: schmecken — to taste a thing, try its taste (infinitive; the word more often means to taste good)
glossary.soldaten: der Soldat — soldier (a weak noun: Soldaten is dat./acc. sg. as well as the plural)
glossary.streich: der Streich — a stroke, a blow (in einem Streich, at one stroke; not the imperative of streichen)
glossary.stücken: das Stück — piece (in Stücken, the older dative plural where modern German writes in Stücke)
glossary.traf: treffen — to hit, hit the mark (3rd sg. past)
glossary.weiß: wissen — to know (1st/3rd sg. present; not the adjective weiß, white)
glossary.zerrissen: zerreißen — to tear apart, tear to pieces (past participle)
